claims.detail: I recomputed this from the answer hashes in the unit files. Across every engine, pass, thread setting, warm call and cold call there were 0 seeds with more than one answer, at 1e-9 and also exactly. This covers primary, S1 and base on both graphs, S2 across LadybugDB settings, and the 20 questions across the three engines. I did not re-run the comparison against the reference arm; that result is taken from icheck.js. 17 of the 200 frozen-graph seeds return an empty answer in every engine; dropping them changes no verdict.

claims.claim: Host load recorded per block; repeated and flagged blocks treated by the rule
claims.detail: No attempt has a repeat or flag decision that disagrees with the rule (other work above 12 of 24 CPUs). All 6 kept-and-flagged blocks are fourth attempts. I re-derived the host share of other work from host_load.jsonl; it agrees within 0.01 CPUs for all 2,000 blocks. The VM share was not saved, so I could not check it. Dropping the 6 flagged blocks changes no verdict. Within the same round the engines saw almost the same load (median difference 0.01 to 0.05 CPUs). The machine was not quiet: other work had a median of 5.8 to 5.9 CPUs and a 90th percentile of about 10 CPUs.

claims.claim: Every 'difference that holds' holds in wall and CPU time and exceeds the spread between passes; nothing inside the noise is stated as a difference
claims.detail: All 149 holds reproduce under the declared rule. In each of them every pass agrees in both wall and CPU time, and the five pass values of the two engines never overlap. However, 45 are duplicates (a best-threads row where both engines' best setting is 1 thread). Another 15 exceed the larger of the two spreads but not the sum of both. The rule is conservative: 9 'inside the noise' comparisons also have non-overlapping pass ranges, for example frozen primary LadybugDB against DuckDB. No noise item is stated as a difference anywhere.

claims.claim: tune/primary 1 thread cold: LadybugDB lower than DuckDB+DuckPGQ by 87.2 ms wall (and the other 12 cold claims where LadybugDB is the lower engine)
claims.detail: These numbers leave out LadybugDB's facts load: a median of 92 ms on the tune graph and 163 to 179 ms on the frozen graph. The LadybugDB arm needs this load to answer; SQLite and DuckDB load nothing. Counted in, DuckDB is lower on tune primary, S1 and base (inside the noise there). DuckDB is lower and the difference holds on frozen primary, S1, base and the questions. The frozen S1 and base 'LadybugDB lower than SQLite' cold claims fall inside the noise. summary.md never says that this load is excluded.

claims.claim: tune/S1 1 thread warm median: LadybugDB lower than SQLite by 98.2 ms; frozen/S1: lower by 239 ms
claims.detail: The numbers reproduce and the difference holds, even with caches dropped (frozen S1: 51.1 ms against 286 ms). It may only be quoted with its label. LadybugDB's PageRank is 40 iterations in JavaScript over a transition CSR cached in application code. SQLite's is about 270 SQL statements per ranking. This compares PageRank implementations, not graph operators.

claims.claim: frozen/primary 1 thread warm median: SQLite lower than LadybugDB by 38.5 ms and lower than DuckDB+DuckPGQ by 66.0 ms
claims.detail: Reproduced: 32.7, 71.2 and 98.7 ms. These hold in all 5 passes. LadybugDB's degree-normalised spreading runs in JavaScript. DuckDB's time includes about 10.3 ms of client round trips.

claims.claim: Label: DuckPGQ's k-hop is recursive SQL, not a graph operator
claims.detail: This is true only for the bounded classes (S1, base). For the unbounded primary, arms/duckpgq/pgq.js khop uses iterativelength() over a CSR plus a GRAPH_TABLE MATCH pattern. The parenthesis in the label says this, but the headline clause is wrong for the primary.

claims.claim: Labels: LadybugDB PageRank in application code over a cached adjacency; SQLite walk is a recursive CTE (unbounded: level loop); primary spreading in JavaScript for LadybugDB
claims.detail: Verified in the code. In lb.js, pprApp loops PPR_ITERS = 40 times, with pprImpl 'app' in bench/ladybug.js. In rel.js, useCte = true for bounded hops and khop_level runs in a JavaScript loop for unbounded hops. In lb.js, degnorm runs Cypher for arcs and degrees and spreads in JavaScript; the reach is the native SHORTEST pattern.

claims.claim: Thread settings stated and read back
claims.detail: The read-back matches the requested setting in every warm block. But 'best' is a single calibration pick taken under load, not a setting shown to be faster. LadybugDB frozen primary 'best 4' was 67.4 ms against 71.2 ms at 1 thread (inside a spread of about 14 to 15 ms) and used about 50 % more CPU. SQLite's question 'best 4' is PRAGMA threads = 3, which adds sorter helper threads only. Builds and updates ran at each engine's default thread count.

claims.claim: Query-class title: LadybugDB S2 'native engine mode'
claims.detail: Per query, S2 runs the native SHORTEST reach, JavaScript PageRank, and a Cypher read of the stored n.comm value. The Louvain grouping comes from build time, read from a stored prior file.

claims.claim: Store build, size and one-file update differences (for example SQLite lower than LadybugDB by 2,795 ms on the tune build)
claims.detail: These reproduce and hold, but they compare the three designs: each arm stores different extra tables and runs at its engine's default threads. LadybugDB's update re-runs page_rank, k-core and Louvain. The LadybugDB build spread is large because one pass took about 5.1 to 5.3 s.

mismatches: summary.md and engines.json never say that LadybugDB's cold figure leaves out the 90 to 180 ms facts load that only the LadybugDB arm needs. Only bench/NOTES.md mentions it. The cold column therefore favours LadybugDB, and 13 'differences that hold' rest on it.

The heading 'Differences that hold' lists 149 statements, but 45 are verbatim repeats of 1-thread statements under 'best threads', where both engines' best setting is 1. There are 104 distinct findings.
Item-20 label 1 says DuckPGQ's k-hop is 'not a graph operator'. For the unbounded primary, the arm reaches nodes with DuckPGQ's iterativelength() over a CSR.

The 'query text' column (LadybugDB primary: 2 statements, 471 characters) counts only the text sent to the engine. It is not the protocol's 'lines of query code per algorithm', because LadybugDB's spreading and PageRank are JavaScript that is not counted.
Protocol section 7 lists memory as an engine measure. Process RSS is recorded in engines.json (rss_mb) but summary.md neither shows nor compares it. It is the RSS of the whole Node process.

The engine host_load record counts calibration blocks (2,098 final, 164 repeats), while summary.md counts passes only (2,000 kept, 148 repeats). Both are correct for their own scope, but the scopes differ.
The harness-IPC row frozen/primary reports a spread of 89.9 ms that comes from one kept-and-flagged block: pass 2, with other work at 19.96 of 24 CPUs.
must_not_claim: Graph engines are faster than SQL (or than SQLite) at answering 'what is connected to this code?'.
SQLite is faster (or slower) than the graph engines in general; the order depends on the configuration and on where each arm runs its ranking.
LadybugDB's graph engine computes PageRank, or the primary ranking, faster: in the LadybugDB arm both run in JavaScript.
The S1 and 2-hop base timings compare a graph operator with SQL: they compare a JavaScript PageRank over an application cache, one recursive SQL statement, and about 270 SQL statements per ranking.
DuckPGQ's graph operators are slower than SQL.
LadybugDB starts cold faster than DuckDB or SQLite: its cold figure leaves out a facts load of about 90 to 180 ms that only it needs.
149 separate differences between the engines hold: 45 of them repeat a 1-thread statement.
The timing was taken on a quiet machine.
A 'best thread setting' is faster than one thread.
LadybugDB needs less query code (2 statements, 471 characters): its algorithm code is JavaScript and is not counted.
Store build time, update time or size on disk measure the engines alone.
These timings show which engine this project should adopt.
An agent finishes tasks faster with any of these stores.
Anything here was timed on held-out tasks or questions.
The timings carry over to larger graphs, other repositories or other machines.
